lessonCandidates: Parallel agents in one worktree need a COMMIT PROTOCOL (git commit --only), not just a file-ownership contract — `git add` swallowed a sibling's staged work.

A permission decision has two stores (daemon + CLI) and a new consent question needs the grant guard in BOTH — daemon-side (TASK-244 consults_grants=false) and client-side (TASK-251 branch above allow_outcome/deny_outcome). Each agent could only see its own half; the deny direction produced a CONFIG WRITE from a grant that said deny.
A one-home sweep that searches for a qualified call (`budget::derive(`) is inert against unqualified imports and multi-line `use` statements — TASK-259's own first draft.

STRONGEST: mutate the guard BEFORE writing its test. TASK-256 found THREE mutations that survived a green 2,343-test suite — including one where an over-budget consent recorded under a skill grant's DIGEST spelling would be invisible to every assertion while fully visible to the door that consults grants, running that skill's commands for the rest of the session with no prompt on any screen. State an invariant about the MAP, not about a key.

A rule that lives only in an ADR paragraph is not a guard. ADR-8 named max_turns/EndTurn as deliberately un-suspended; widening the exception to cover them passed all 2,343 tests, because the accepted turn still succeeds and only the NEXT turn inherits an unbounded conversation.
A one-home sweep must be daemon-wide and NAME its unrelated collisions, not retreat from them — the narrowed sweep did not cover the very code this REQ added.

Parallel agents in ONE worktree share a cargo target dir: concurrent rebuilds can CORRUPT e2e test binaries, not merely produce confusing results (TASK-252 discarded a whole run for this). Combined with the shared-index race and the stale-daemon trap, one worktree needs three protocols, not one: commit with `git commit --only`, treat any mid-phase failure as suspect until re-run in isolation, and build the workspace before any targeted test.

phase4.ownerDecisionBR14_1: TASK-249 found BR-14.1's withdrawal is UNOBSERVABLE: run_prompt_turn's failure arm calls CarriedTurn::abandon, which writes nothing, so the session already returns to what it was and the expansion never enters it. AC-22 is true by construction; no test distinguishes withdraw_block from its deletion (LESSON-544). TASK-249 made the withdrawal COMMIT on that one path so it is observable — which NARROWS REQ-567 BR-6 (a failed turn now mutates the session). ORCHESTRATOR RECOMMENDATION: revert to abandon and STRIKE BR-14.1's mechanism — when code is unobservable because the guarantee already holds, delete the code rather than change semantics to justify it. BR-14.2's memo already delivers the residual value. This is REQ-567's invariant, so it needs the owner.

phase4.evidenceForBR14_1: TASK-257 MEASURED it: THREE independent mechanisms already remove the expansion from the next turn — the failure arm abandons, REQ-586 BR-10's budget re-assertion drops the oversized block AT THE COMMIT, and ordinary pressure drops it again next turn. Its control test proves the expansion is gone even on the path where the turn SERVES and nothing is withdrawn. So the withdrawal's ONLY unique contribution is leaving the REFUSAL in the conversation — which is what TASK-249 had to narrow REQ-567 BR-6 to make observable. Phase 5 should weigh whether that record is worth the narrowing, given BR-14.2's memo already carries the same fact into the next offer.
